tagline: River valleys and a rolling plateau connect Celina with Cumberland Gap.
intro: Tennessee’s Cumberland National Scenic Byway crosses farmland, mountain forest and the rolling tableland of the Cumberland Plateau. The Upper Cumberland Development District presents it as a connection between historic rural landscapes and frontier culture. Edwin Gardner’s route narrative describes a 21-mile climb on TN 63 through the Cumberland Mountains and a six-mile I-75 link past the rock ribs of Devil’s Racetrack. In Powell Valley, Gardner places the road between farmland along the Powell River and an escarpment rising 1,000 feet or more.

Movement through the region long predates the modern byway: by 1790, settlers traveled through Cumberland Gap on trails already used by Native Americans and wildlife. At the western end, Celina received timber floated down the Obey, then rafted onward to Nashville. Road alignments have changed too. TN 52 passed through Rugby until a bypass opened in December 2013.

Traveling east from Celina, the route reaches Livingston and Byrdstown, then the Wolf River valley and Alvin York’s farm near Pall Mall. US 127 leads south to Jamestown, followed by TN 52 toward Allardt and Rugby. Beyond Rugby, the corridor uses US 27 and TN 63, then I-75 toward Cove Lake. The final valley stretch follows Powell Valley Road to US 25E just south of Cumberland Gap.

moments.title: Celina
moments.text: The Obey reaches the Cumberland at Celina, where a river junction once supported a logging town. In the late nineteenth century, logs cut in forests to the east floated down the Obey to town. From Celina, timber rafts traveled on to Nashville. The rivers here are now part of Cordell Hull Lake, while Dale Hollow Dam lies upstream on the Obey, east of town. The original Clay County courthouse survives from 1873. The town occupies a broad valley at the meeting of the rivers, surrounded by the rugged hills of the eastern Highland Rim.

moments.title: Alvin York farm and gristmill
moments.text: Alvin York accepted a home in Pall Mall after rejecting most early offers to profit from his wartime fame. The Nashville Rotary Club bought the farm on promissory notes in 1919, funded a house, and transferred the land to York after paying off the notes in 1922. The mill came separately: York bought it in 1943. Built around 1880, its frame millhouse rests on stacked-rock pillars beside the Wolf River. Water diverted through a millrace once turned a large turbine. The mill is no longer operational. House, mill and post office lie along US 127.

moments.title: Rugby
moments.text: Rugby’s buildings include both survivors of an English settlement experiment and later reconstructions. Thomas Hughes founded the colony in 1880, seeking land ownership and cooperative life for younger sons of the English gentry. Poor soil, unfamiliar manual labor, disputed land titles and an 1881 typhoid outbreak undermined the experiment. Historic Rugby formed in 1966 to preserve surviving structures, including Christ Church and the Thomas Hughes Library. The Board of Aid office and Rugby Commissary are reconstructions based on original designs. The library, built in 1882, retains most of its original collection of books.
